subtopic_detail: Daytime sleep attacks with knee buckling on laughter in a nineteen year old whose sleep diary shows eight hours nightly
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old apprentice who has fallen asleep at his workbench three times in the past month and was nearly stood down after dozing off during a safety briefing. He says the sleepiness comes on suddenly and that a ten minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours.

He has twice felt his knees give way while laughing with his friends, staying fully aware throughout and recovering within a minute. He sometimes cannot move for a few seconds as he wakes. A two week sleep diary shows a consistent bedtime with eight hours of sleep each night, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. He scores 3 on a depression screening questionnaire and describes his mood as good.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1 oropharynx, no goitre, normal cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examination, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 88 micrograms/L (30 to 300), Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24, two week actigraphy confirms eight hours of sleep nightly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Hypersomnia does occur in depression, but he screens negative, describes his mood as good and wakes refreshed from naps, whereas depressive hypersomnia is typically unrefreshing. Serotonergic agents are used in this condition for cataplexy rather than as an initial empirical trial. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start modafinil now and arrange a sleep study if there is no response
options.rationale: Starting a wake promoting agent before the sleep study contaminates the multiple sleep latency test, which must be performed off stimulants, and in Australia subsidised access depends on a confirmed diagnosis. Treating first also leaves the driving and workplace safety assessment without a diagnosis to rest on. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange thyroid function and iron studies, then review in four weeks
options.rationale: These are reasonable screening tests for fatigue, but they have already been done and are normal, and neither explains sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion. Repeating normal investigations delays the study that establishes the diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sudden emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with preserved awareness, refreshing naps, sleep paralysis and severe daytime sleepiness despite adequate nocturnal sleep is the pattern of narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes followed by a multiple sleep latency test. A mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods confirms it. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and review him again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene advice addresses insufficient or irregular sleep, which the diary and actigraphy have already excluded by documenting eight consistent hours nightly. The near pair here is insufficient sleep syndrome, which is far commoner in this age group but does not produce cataplexy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: Excessive daytime sleepiness in a young adult is most often caused by insufficient or irregular sleep, and a sleep diary with actigraphy is what separates that from a primary hypersomnia. Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the hypothalamus and is defined clinically by sleepiness with cataplexy, a sudden partial or complete loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, during which the person remains fully conscious. Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep complete the tetrad but are individually non specific, and cataplexy is the feature that carries real diagnostic weight. Diagnosis in Australia requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test performed off stimulants and antidepressants, which is why treatment is not started first.
key_points: Cataplexy with preserved awareness is the most specific clinical feature
Refreshing short naps distinguish this from depressive hypersomnia
A sleep diary excludes insufficient sleep as the explanation
The multiple sleep latency test must be performed off stimulants
Diagnosis precedes treatment because access and driving advice both depend on it
explanation.pearls: Cataplexy is frequently misread as syncope or as a seizure, and the discriminator at the bedside is that consciousness is fully retained throughout the attack, so a patient who can recount what was said while they were slumped on the floor has had cataplexy rather than a faint.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a woman living in Hobart
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who has come in each of the last four Junes with the same complaint. She describes flat mood, sleeping ten to eleven hours and still feeling leaden, craving bread and sweet food, and gaining four or five kilograms over the winter that she loses again by December.

She moved to Hobart five years ago from Cairns. Her mood and energy are entirely normal from about October to April, and she has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased activity. She works indoors and leaves for work and returns home in the dark through winter. She is not suicidal, functions at work with effort, and her weight and sleep are the symptoms she most wants addressed.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg per square metre, no goitre, no tremor, affect reactive during the consultation, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, ferritin 65 micrograms/L (30 to 200), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 46 nmol/L (greater than 50), Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 14 out of 27

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her current episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser and arrange monitoring of the levels
options.rationale: Lithium is used where there is a bipolar diathesis, and she has never had an episode of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased goal directed activity. A seasonal pattern alone does not make a depressive illness bipolar. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start high dose oral cholecalciferol and review her mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Her vitamin D level is only marginally below the target and supplementation has not been shown to treat depressive episodes, seasonal or otherwise. Correcting the level is reasonable for bone health but is not a treatment for the presenting problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment at the local mental health unit
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for severe, treatment resistant, psychotic or life threatening depression, and she is working, eating and not suicidal with a moderate symptom score. Offering it at this stage is disproportionate to the severity. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise increased outdoor exercise alone and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Exercise and daylight exposure are worth encouraging but a three month review takes her to the end of winter, by which time the episode would have remitted regardless of what was done. The near pair here is that morning outdoor light is genuinely useful, but as an adjunct rather than as the whole plan. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start bright light therapy each morning and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern and the atypical features of hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain respond to bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes soon after waking, with benefit usually apparent within one to two weeks. It is recommended first for moderate seasonal episodes because it works quickly, is well tolerated, and can be started before the winter in subsequent years to prevent recurrence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive episodes rather than a separate diagnosis, and it requires episodes that begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years with no non seasonal episodes in between. The symptom profile is characteristically atypical, with hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving, weight gain and leaden heaviness, in contrast to the insomnia and weight loss of melancholic depression. Prevalence rises with latitude, so the pattern is far more common in Tasmania than in northern Queensland, and a recent move south is a genuinely relevant piece of history. Bright light therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for the seasonal pattern, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors all have evidence, and treatment can be started prophylactically in early autumn once the pattern is established.
key_points: The seasonal specifier requires at least two consecutive years of the same pattern
Hypersomnia with carbohydrate craving and weight gain is the typical profile
Absence of any elevated mood episode argues against a bipolar diathesis
Bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes after waking is the usual regimen
Prophylactic treatment can be started before the season in later years
explanation.pearls: Bright light therapy should be given within an hour of waking rather than in the evening, because evening exposure delays the circadian phase and can worsen the hypersomnia the treatment is meant to relieve.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal affective disorder

subtopic_detail: Emotional exhaustion and cynicism in a surgical registrar whose symptoms lift entirely on annual leave and who has no impairment at work
stem:
You are a general practitioner and a 31 year old surgical registrar has booked a long appointment with you as her own doctor. She describes eight months of dreading the drive to work, feeling she has nothing left to give her patients, and finding herself short and impatient at handover in a way that is unlike her.

She took two weeks of leave in July, felt like herself again by the fifth day, and the dread returned within a week of going back. Her sleep is normal on days off, she is eating normally and she still enjoys her netball team and her friends. She has had no thoughts of self harm, drinks two standard drinks on a Friday night and takes no medication. She has never made a clinical error she is aware of, is not the subject of any complaint, and says she would step back immediately if she thought a patient was at risk.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when describing work but reactive affect with normal rapport, no psychomotor change, cognition intact, no thoughts of self harm or harm to others
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 8 out of 27, Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7 score 6 out of 21, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test consumption score 3, full blood count and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange structured review with workload focused counselling and no notification
options.rationale: Her symptoms are work bound, remit fully on leave and are accompanied by preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite elsewhere, which describes occupational burnout rather than a major depressive episode, and the intervention that works is directed at workload, recovery and role rather than at the person alone. The mandatory notification threshold requires that a practitioner is placing the public at substantial risk of harm through an impairment, and a registrar who is functioning safely, has insight and is engaging in treatment does not meet it. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.text: Make a mandatory notification to the regulator and arrange to review her
options.rationale: Mandatory notification is triggered by impairment, intoxication, significant departure from accepted standards or sexual misconduct placing the public at substantial risk, none of which is present in a practitioner who is working safely and seeking help. Notifying in these circumstances deters doctors from disclosing distress, which is the harm the threshold is set to avoid. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment is directed at a depressive episode, and her symptoms remit completely on leave with preserved anhedonia free enjoyment, sleep and appetite, which is not that illness. Medicating a workload problem leaves the cause untouched and can delay the changes that would help. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Certify her as unfit for work for three months and review her after that
options.rationale: Prolonged certified absence without a formal diagnosis or a plan to change the work conditions usually leads to the same symptoms recurring on return, as her own two week experience demonstrates. Time away helps only when it is paired with a change in the demands she returns to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer her to the hospital employee assistance programme and take no further action
options.rationale: An employee assistance programme is a useful adjunct but a single referral without continuing review leaves no one tracking whether she deteriorates into a depressive episode. The near pair here is that ongoing review by her own general practitioner is what distinguishes adequate care from a referral made and forgotten. (Source: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners)
source_refs: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners

explanation.summary: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon characterised by emotional exhaustion, cynicism or depersonalisation, and reduced professional efficacy, and it is classified as a factor influencing health status rather than as a mental disorder. The clinical task is to separate it from a major depressive episode, because the treatments differ, and the most useful discriminator is context dependence, since burnout remits away from the workplace while a depressive episode follows the person everywhere. The two overlap and burnout is a risk factor for depression, so a doctor presenting this way needs ongoing review rather than a single assessment. Doctors seeking care for their own mental health face a specific additional barrier in the fear of mandatory notification, and Australian guidance is explicit that treating practitioners notify only where there is substantial risk of harm to the public from impairment, not merely because a colleague is unwell.
key_points: Burnout remits away from work whereas a depressive episode does not
Preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite argue against major depression
Effective intervention targets workload and role, not only the individual
Mandatory notification requires substantial risk of harm from impairment
Burnout is a risk factor for depression, so continuing review is required
explanation.pearls: Every practitioner should have their own general practitioner and should not self prescribe or be treated by a colleague informally, because self treatment is associated with delayed presentation and with the under recognition of deterioration that turns burnout into a depressive episode.

sources.label: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners
RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Weight loss in a twelve year old boy restricting by food texture since toddlerhood with no body image concern or fear of weight gain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 12 year old boy referred because he has lost 4 kg over six months and his weight has fallen from the 25th to below the 3rd centile. His parents say he has eaten only about eight foods since he was three, all of them beige and dry, and that anything wet, mixed or lumpy makes him gag.

He says he would like to be bigger and stronger so he can make the football team, and that he does not think he is fat. He has no fear of gaining weight, does not check his body in the mirror, does not exercise to burn energy and has never made himself vomit. The range of foods he accepts has narrowed further this year after he choked on a piece of apple. He has no abdominal pain, no diarrhoea and opens his bowels normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 52 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Weight below the 3rd centile having previously tracked the 25th, height on the 25th centile, Tanner stage 1, no lanugo, no parotid swelling, no dental erosion, no Russell sign on the knuckles
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, coeliac serology negative with normal total immunoglobulin A, C reactive protein within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, zinc and iron studies show mild iron deficiency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is ordinary fussy eating and review in a year
options.rationale: Ordinary selective eating does not cause a fall across centiles, weight loss and bradycardia, and this presentation meets the threshold for a feeding and eating disorder. A year of observation would allow further growth failure and pubertal delay. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Start family based treatment for anorexia nervosa with weekly weighing
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the evidence based approach for anorexia nervosa, which requires a fear of weight gain or behaviour that interferes with it, and he wants to gain weight and has no body image disturbance. Applying a treatment built around challenging a drive for thinness to a sensory and choking based avoidance misses the mechanism. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Refer to a paediatric eating disorder service with dietitian involvement
options.rationale: Restriction driven by sensory characteristics of food and by fear of choking, without body image disturbance or fear of weight gain, and producing weight loss with nutritional deficiency, is avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, which is managed by a multidisciplinary eating disorder service with dietetic and psychological input. Treatment uses graded exposure to new textures alongside nutritional restoration rather than the approaches designed for weight and shape concerns. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude an organic cause
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated where there is dysphagia, food impaction, reflux symptoms or suspicion of eosinophilic disease, and his symptoms are texture aversion from toddlerhood rather than difficulty with swallowing itself. Coeliac serology and inflammatory markers are already normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

options.text: Start fluoxetine for restrictive eating and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: No medication has an established role as primary treatment for this disorder, and antidepressants in underweight children carry particular monitoring requirements without addressing the avoidance. The near pair here is that fluoxetine does have a role in bulimia nervosa in adults, which is a different disorder entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder is defined by a persistent failure to meet nutritional or energy needs leading to weight loss, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or marked psychosocial interference, in the absence of body image disturbance or a drive for thinness. Three patterns are described, namely sensory sensitivity to the appearance, smell or texture of food, lack of interest in eating, and fear of an aversive consequence such as choking or vomiting, and children commonly show more than one, as this boy does. It is distinguished from ordinary selective eating by the presence of that nutritional or functional impact, and from anorexia nervosa by the absence of weight and shape concerns, which is why the specific questions about fear of weight gain and body checking matter. Medical instability is assessed exactly as it would be in any restrictive eating disorder, since bradycardia, hypotension and electrolyte disturbance carry the same significance whatever the motivation for the restriction.
key_points: The disorder is defined by nutritional impact without weight or shape concern
Sensory, low appetite and aversive consequence patterns often coexist
Bradycardia in an underweight child signals medical instability regardless of diagnosis
Family based treatment for anorexia nervosa is not the correct model here
Treatment combines graded texture exposure with nutritional restoration
explanation.pearls: A resting heart rate below 50 beats per minute, a postural blood pressure drop of more than 20 mmHg, or a temperature below 35.5 degrees Celsius in a child with restrictive eating are indications for medical admission regardless of which eating disorder is causing the restriction.

sources.label: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards
BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

subtopic_detail: Eight months of not speaking at school in a six year old who talks fluently at home and passed school hearing screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old girl whose teacher has written a letter because she has not spoken a word at school since she started in February. Her parents bring a phone video in which she is chatting and singing at home with her younger brother, using full sentences and a wide vocabulary.

At school she nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and she will speak to no one, including other children. She played normally in the waiting room but has not spoken to you during the consultation, standing close to her mother and answering by nodding. Her school hearing screening in March was normal. Her parents describe her as shy with strangers since she was a toddler but say she has always spoken freely with family.

data_table.Examination: Well grown child, alert and engaged with toys, makes intermittent eye contact and uses gesture and pointing appropriately, no speech during consultation, no dysmorphic features, normal gait and coordination
data_table.Investigations: School hearing screening normal, growth and development otherwise age appropriate, no formal language assessment yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for formal audiology assessment before considering any other referral
options.rationale: Hearing loss is a reasonable consideration for a child who does not speak, but she has passed screening and, more decisively, speaks fluently and sings at home, which requires intact hearing. Repeating the hearing assessment delays the referral that addresses the anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer to a speech pathologist for assessment of a developmental language disorder
options.rationale: A developmental language disorder affects language in every setting, whereas her vocabulary and sentence structure are age appropriate at home on the video her parents have brought. Speech pathology may join the team later, but the primary problem is situational anxiety rather than language competence. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is shyness and review her again in twelve months
options.rationale: Eight months of complete absence of speech in a whole setting is well beyond situational shyness and beyond the one month threshold that defines the disorder. Untreated, the pattern becomes entrenched and predicts later social anxiety disorder and academic underachievement. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with a graded school based programme
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in a specific setting for more than a month, with fluent speech elsewhere, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder for which behavioural treatment using graded exposure and stimulus fading delivered in the school environment is first line. Involving the teacher matters because progress depends on changing how adults in the setting respond, and pressuring the child to speak reliably makes it worse. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Start a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Medication is considered when a structured behavioural programme has been tried and has not produced progress, or where impairment is severe, and it is an adjunct rather than a first step in a six year old. The near pair here is that fluoxetine does have evidence in this disorder, but after behavioural treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child who speaks normally in some settings consistently fails to speak in specific social situations where speech is expected, most often school, for at least one month beyond the first month of attendance. It is frequently misread as oppositional behaviour, as shyness or as a language or hearing problem, and the demonstration that the child speaks fluently somewhere is what settles those questions. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a minority have a coexisting language or communication difficulty, so assessment includes both. Treatment is behavioural, using graded exposure, stimulus fading and shaping delivered largely in the setting where the child is mute, with the adults around the child coached not to pressure or to speak for them, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors reserved for cases that do not respond.
key_points: Fluent speech in one setting excludes hearing loss and language disorder
The diagnostic threshold is one month beyond the first month of school
Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in most affected children
Treatment is delivered in the setting where the child does not speak
Pressuring the child to speak reliably worsens the avoidance
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the core technique, in which the child first speaks to a trusted person in the empty classroom and a peer or teacher is then gradually introduced into the room, because the aim is to transfer existing speech into the feared setting rather than to teach speech the child already has.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

subtopic_detail: An evening urge to move the legs relieved by walking in a man on risperidone whose ferritin is 22 micrograms per litre
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46 year old man with schizophrenia who has been on the same dose of risperidone for three years without change. He complains of a crawling discomfort deep in both calves that builds while he is watching television after dinner and is worst when he first gets into bed.

Walking around the flat relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns when he sits back down. He has no symptoms in the morning or at work, and he is no more restless in the waiting room now than at any previous review. His partner says his legs jerk repeatedly in the first hours of sleep. He has had heavy nosebleeds this year and his diet is limited.

data_table.Examination: No akathisic pacing or inability to remain seated during a 20 minute interview, no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor, no abnormal involuntary movements of the face or tongue, normal power and reflexes in both legs with intact pinprick and vibration sense
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130 to 180), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (16 to 45), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting glucose within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Add propranolol for akathisia and review his symptoms in two weeks
options.rationale: Akathisia is a subjective restlessness of the whole body that is present throughout the day, is not confined to the legs, is not relieved by brief walking and typically follows a dose increase or a recent start. He has been on an unchanged dose for three years and sits still throughout the interview. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and investigate the cause of the iron loss
options.rationale: An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations that worsen at rest in the evening, are relieved by movement and are accompanied by periodic limb movements describes restless legs syndrome, and iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause with replacement indicated when ferritin is below about 75 micrograms per litre. The nosebleeds and restricted diet need their own assessment, since treating the deficiency without finding its source leaves the cause unaddressed. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Add benztropine at night and review his symptoms again in two weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents treat drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, neither of which is present on examination, and they are ineffective for this circadian urge to move. They also worsen cognition and carry a risk of aggravating tardive movements. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start a dopamine agonist at night and review his symptoms in two weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists do treat the syndrome but are no longer first line because of augmentation, in which symptoms intensify and spread over months of treatment, and they should not be started before reversible causes are corrected. The near pair here is that they remain an option once iron is replete and symptoms persist. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose and review his symptoms again in two weeks
options.rationale: Reducing an effective antipsychotic that has maintained him for three years risks relapse of psychosis, and the symptom pattern here is not the dose related akathisia that a reduction would target. Antipsychotics can aggravate the syndrome, but iron correction is tried before destabilising treatment that is working. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically on five features, namely an urge to move the legs usually with uncomfortable sensations, worsening at rest, relief with movement, a circadian pattern worst in the evening or at night, and the absence of a better explanation such as cramp or positional discomfort. It is commonly confused with akathisia in psychiatric patients, and the discriminators are that akathisia is generalised rather than confined to the legs, lacks the evening predominance, is not relieved by brief walking, and is temporally linked to starting or increasing a dopamine blocking drug. Periodic limb movements of sleep, described by a bed partner as repeated leg jerks, accompany the syndrome in most patients and support the diagnosis. Iron deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy and dopamine blocking or serotonergic drugs are the secondary causes to look for, and iron status should be checked in every patient because replacement can abolish symptoms entirely.
key_points: The five clinical criteria include a circadian pattern and relief with movement
Akathisia is generalised and follows a dose change, unlike this pattern
Periodic limb movements reported by a partner support the diagnosis
Replacement is indicated at a ferritin below about 75 micrograms per litre
Reversible causes are corrected before starting symptomatic drug therapy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for iron replacement in restless legs syndrome is around 75 micrograms per litre, which is well above the level at which iron deficiency anaemia is diagnosed, so a normal haemoglobin with a ferritin in the 20s is still an indication to treat.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome
BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome
